newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIAN EXOTICS - Regionals ignore Deng, track dollar.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN EXOTICS - Regionals ignore Deng, track dollar.

text.p: Southeast Asian currencies were largely unmoved by the death of Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping overnight, with most regionals taking their cue from movements in the dollar/majors, dealers said on Thursday.

"It seems the market is well prepared for this piece of news. I think it's just come as a kind of relief for most people. Maybe it's the last piece of negative news," said a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore.
Even the Singapore dollar, which normally benefits from "safe haven" flows on any signs of instability in the region, remained relatively soft against its U.S. counterpart, he said.
In Indonesia, some dealers said the dollar was briefly bought in early trade on the back of Deng's death, but this was quickly countered by offshore selling.
Spot rupiah was quoted at 2,386.50/88.50 at 0425 GMT from a low of 2,389.0. It opened at 2,389.5/90.0.
"Deng's death is big news, but for us here the liquidity issue is more important. The market is driven by liquidity at present," said a foreign bank dealer in Jakarta.
Dealers said anticipation of tighter liquidity on Friday drove tom/next swaps up to a high of 1.7 points before settling down at 1.00/1.05 in mid-morning.
A U.S. bank dealer said Singapore operators appeared to be rather panicky on anticipation of Friday liquidity which sparked off sharp rises in tom/next swaps.
Elsewhere, the Malaysian ringgit climbed back from below the 2.4900 level against the dollar as the U.S. unit lost ground against the majors, dealers said.
Dealer said the early ringgit weakness was caused by dollar shortcovering and a mild move from the ringgit to the Singapore dollar due to Deng's death.
"There was ringgit/Sing selling in the morning on the back of Deng's death. But it did not last," said a dealer with a European bank in Singapore.
"There was selling above 2.4910, but dollar is well supported at 2.4850," said a dealer with another European bank in Singapore.

He said sentiment was in favour of the ringgit, particularly after a Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) official said on Tuesday Singapore was not concerned by its currency's weakness against the U.S. dollar.
"That is being viewed as a tacit approval for the Singapore dollar to decline," the dealer said. "So everybody is bullish ringgit/Sing," he added.
The Singapore dollar showed no immediate reaction to trade data showing a 3.1 percent year-on-year drop in January non-oil domestic exports.
Most economists had expected the January figure to show flat growth as it was off a very high base last year.
MMS International said in a market commentary the figure was relatively healthy and not expected to have a negative impact on the market.
"However, it does show that the recovery is patchy at best, with no clear signs of a strong rebound," MMS said.
The U.S. bank dealer said the Singapore dollar was undergoing a consolidation after its sharp drop on the back of the MAS official's statement on Tuesday.
"I think people are looking to buy dollar/Sing at 1.4240," he said. The U.S. dollar faced commercial selling pressure around S$1.4285/90, slowing its rise to the S$1.4300 target, he added.
The Thai baht was slightly weaker as players covered their short dollar positions.
The baht was quoted at 26.000/26.020 to the dollar at 0425 GMT against 25.998/26.008 late on Wednesday. The Bank of Thailand fixed the baht/dollar mid-rate unchanged at 25.98 per dollar.
The U.S. bank dealer said the baht did not react to vague rumours of a Thai newspaper report that international financier George Soros was planning an attack on the baht.
"We didn't see any (dollar) buying from speculators at all and the dollar/baht didn't react to the news," he said.
-- Madhav Reddy in KL (603-230 8911), Mantik Kusjanto in Jakarta (6221-384-6364), Anuchit Nguyen in Bangkok (662-652-0642) and Sonali Desai in Singapore (65-8703090)
